c.tagline: Myanmar's last royal capital, a plain of golden pagodas and teak monasteries.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are not metered — agree the fare in kyat before you get in. Bring plenty of cash (crisp, unmarked US dollars for exchange, and small kyat notes); cards are rarely accepted and ATMs are unreliable. Grab works in the city.

emergency.note: 199 reaches the police and 192 the ambulance/emergency medical service; 191 is the fire brigade.

avoid.reason: Check current advisories before any trip — armed conflict affects much of the surrounding region, so avoid travel beyond the city, military sites and any protest gatherings.
Curfews, checkpoints and power cuts can appear with little notice; keep a low profile after dark and carry ID.

hood_desc: The bustling downtown grid of numbered streets around Zegyo Market, where most budget guesthouses, money changers, teahouses and street food cluster; central, chaotic and walkable, the natural base for first-timers.

The northeast quarter beneath Mandalay Hill, home to the reconstructed Royal Palace inside its moated walls, Kuthodaw Pagoda (the 'world's largest book'), Sandamuni and the teak Shwenandaw Monastery; the sightseeing heart of the city.

A dense commercial and residential township south of the centre built around the revered Mahamuni Buddha Temple, with gold-leaf workshops, markets and stone-carving streets; busy and authentically local.
A sprawling southern township toward the highway bus terminal and the airport road, quieter and more spread-out, with some upscale resorts and leafier residential streets.

The historic former capital just south of Mandalay, famous for the 1.2 km teak U Bein Bridge over Taungthaman Lake, silk-weaving workshops and sunset crowds; a laid-back day-trip base steeped in old royal Ava.

water.note: Drink only bottled or purified water.

transit.hours: Buses and shared pickups run roughly from dawn to around 8–9:00 PM; after dark most travellers rely on Grab, taxis or motorbike taxis.
transit.note: The cheapest way around is the shared pickup truck (line-car), flagged down along fixed routes; trishaws are handy for short central hops. Traffic is busy but calmer than Yangon, and bicycles are a popular way to tour the flat city.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (small kyat notes) to the conductor on city buses and shared pickup trucks; trishaws and motorbike taxis are negotiated per ride. There is no transit card or metro.

bus: Kywe Se Kan (Chanmyathazi) Highway Bus Terminal — coaches to Yangon, Bagan, Inle Lake and Pyin Oo Lwin
ferry: Ayeyarwady (Irrawaddy) River ferries to Mingun and downriver to Bagan
train: Mandalay Central Railway Station — Myanmar Railways to Yangon, Bagan (Nyaung-U), and the scenic Gokteik Viaduct line to Pyin Oo Lwin, Hsipaw and Lashio

transit.m: Shared taxi to the city centre (~1 hr)
Airline courtesy shuttle bus to downtown (with valid ticket)

tip.r: Not traditionally expected, but small tips for guides, drivers and hotel staff are increasingly appreciated; rounding up is fine.

landmarks: U Bein Bridge
The world's longest teak footbridge stretches 1.2 kilometers across Taungthaman Lake, where silhouetted monks and fishermen create Myanmar's most famous sunset photograph.
Mandalay Hill
A 240-meter stairway pilgrimage past shrines and Buddha statues culminates in Sutaungpyei Pagoda's mirrored terraces and panoramic sunset views over the royal city.
Mandalay Palace
The moated, walled seat of Myanmar's last kings, its reconstructed crimson-and-gold throne halls evoke the lost splendor of the Konbaung dynasty.
Kuthodaw Pagoda
Dubbed the world's biggest book, 729 marble slabs inscribed with the entire Buddhist canon stand in whitewashed shrines around a gilded stupa.
Mahamuni Buddha Temple
Myanmar's second-holiest shrine houses a bronze Buddha so revered that generations of gold-leaf offerings have thickened its body by centimeters.
Shwenandaw Monastery (Golden Palace Monastery)
The sole surviving building of the original royal palace, this teak monastery drips with some of Myanmar's most intricate 19th-century woodcarving.
Mingun Pahtodawgyi
An unfinished brick colossus upriver from Mandalay, cracked dramatically by earthquakes, that would have been the world's largest stupa beside its 90-ton bell.
Sagaing Hill
Across the Irrawaddy, hundreds of white-and-gold pagodas and monasteries cascade down forested slopes in Myanmar's most important center of Buddhist study.
Sandamuni Pagoda
Neighbor to Kuthodaw, its forest of slender white spires shelters 1,774 marble slabs of Buddhist commentaries and a huge iron Buddha image.
Inwa (Ava) Ancient City
Reached by ferry and explored by horse cart, this former royal capital scatters teak monasteries, a leaning watchtower and crumbling stupas among rice fields.

dom.op: Myanmar Railways — tickets at Mandalay Central Railway Station

train.note: Mandalay Central station on 78th Street is the hub of the northern network: overnight trains from Yangon take around 15 hours, from about USD15 for a hard seat to roughly USD50 for an air-conditioned sleeper on the Dagon Mann Express, and daily services run east to Pyin Oo Lwin, Hsipaw and Lashio across the Gokteik viaduct and north to Myitkyina, a bone-shaking 24 hours or more on old stock. Tickets are sold at station counters, generally only a few days ahead, sometimes at a separate foreigner fare, and online booking is unreliable. There is no international passenger rail - the line towards China at Muse was never completed and no trains cross any Myanmar border. Services are frequently cancelled, delayed or rerouted because of the conflict, so confirm locally on the day.

bus.note: Almost all long-distance coaches use the Kwe Se Kan (Chan Mya Shwe Pyi) highway bus station on the southern outskirts, 30-45 minutes from the centre by taxi; shared pickups run into town from the gate. Night buses from Yangon take 8.5-9 hours and cost roughly 10,500 kyat for standard air-conditioned seats or about 16,000 for luxury, and day minibuses serve Bagan, Kalaw, Inle Lake and Hsipaw. JJ Express (https://jjexpress.net/) and Elite Express are the best-known VIP operators and sell online or through agents. There are no scheduled international coaches: the Muse-Ruili crossing into China and the Tachileik crossing into Thailand are restricted, and long stretches of the road network are affected by fighting.

intl.to: Bagan / Nyaung U (Myanmar) - express boat downstream from the Gawein jetty, ~9-11 hr, seasonal
intl.op: private Ayeyarwady express-boat operators — tickets through Mandalay hotels and agents

intl.to: Katha & Bhamo (Myanmar) - upstream slow boats from the Mandalay jetties, 2-3 days
intl.op: Inland Water Transport (IWT) — tickets at the jetty

intl.to: Mingun (Myanmar) - local ferry from the Mayan Chan jetty at the end of 26th Street, ~1 hr upstream
intl.op: local boat operators — tickets at the jetty

ferry.note: Mandalay sits on the Ayeyarwady and the river is still a working transport corridor. The tourist run downstream to Bagan takes 9-11 hours on a fast boat and only operates when the water is high enough, broadly October to March; upstream trips to Katha and Bhamo on government Inland Water Transport vessels take two to three days and are very basic, with deck space rather than cabins. The Mingun boat leaves mid-morning and returns in the early afternoon, a short and popular excursion. All services are domestic, and river schedules have been badly disrupted since 2021 - book through a hotel or agent who can confirm the boat is actually sailing.

full.name: Pyin Oo Lwin
full.blurb: A former British hill station about two hours east with botanical gardens, colonial villas, and horse-drawn carriage rides.

full.name: Anisakan Falls
full.blurb: A three-tiered waterfall near Pyin Oo Lwin reached by a steep jungle trail, about three hours from Mandalay.
